text: Everything in the last two lessons ran through AI Builder's prompt builder — Microsoft's wrapper around a generative model. That wrapper is convenient, but it isn't the only path, because prompt builder's prompts are powered by Azure OpenAI Service underneath, and you can reach that same model family more directly too.

There are three layers to the same underlying model family. AI Builder prompts are the simplest — you write instructions, AI Builder handles the connection. Azure OpenAI Service is the actual resource hosting the model underneath. And Azure AI Services is the wider family Azure OpenAI belongs to, alongside things like Azure AI Language and the Document Intelligence service that already powers AI Builder's document processing from lesson eight.

A direct call is nothing more than the same HTTP action from chapter one, posting to your Azure OpenAI resource's chat completions endpoint. The body is JSON — a system instruction, a user message built from dynamic content — and the reply comes back nested inside the response, parsed with Parse JSON exactly like any other API.

If prompt builder is still the right fit but you haven't built the prompt yet, you don't have to leave the flow designer — selecting Run a prompt, then New custom prompt, opens prompt builder right on the spot.

Whichever layer generates the text, Microsoft's own guidance is the same: have a person review AI-generated output before it's treated as final, especially anything customer-facing. In a flow, that's usually a Start and wait for an approval of text action, right after the prompt or HTTP call.

The reviewer's decision, not the raw model output, is what the rest of the flow actually acts on. Chapter three goes much further into this pattern with Copilot Studio agents — this is the Power Automate-only version of the same idea.
Next, lesson thirteen: putting this entire chapter together into one end-to-end AI-powered document processing flow for Castlebridge Logistics.
